summary: Help 11–12 year-olds distinguish mass (the amount of matter, in kg, unchanged by location) from weight (the gravitational force on that matter, in N, W = m×g), using the same object on two instruments — a two-pan balance compared against standard masses (kg) and a spring scale/newton meter (N) — and comparing readings across Earth, Moon and Jupiter. Define weight operationally (what a spring scale reads) rather than arguing against the 'heaviness is a property' intuition head-on, and teach alongside gravity because the two conflate. Expect only partial mastery at this age.
misconceptions: Mass and weight are interchangeable words for the same property (the core error; ~56% define weight as 'heavy or light'; persists into adulthood)
Weight is a fixed property of the object that doesn't change with location — or, conversely, that mass AND weight both shrink equally on the Moon
Confusing the units — treating kg as a unit of weight/force (reinforced by grocery packaging putting grams beside force units)
A balance and a spring scale 'measure the same thing'
Entangled gravity errors: no gravity in space → no weight and no mass; gravity needs air
Carryover that 'more mass' is why heavier things fall faster

activities.title: Two instruments, one rock, different planets
steps: Place the SAME object (e.g. a 2 kg rock) on two instruments side by side: a two-pan (equal-arm) balance that compares the rock against standard kilogram masses, and a spring scale/newton meter that reads in newtons. On Earth note the rock balances 2 kg of standard masses and the spring scale reads about 20 N. (A digital scale that shows kg actually senses force and is set up for Earth's g, so on the Moon it would read too low. Only a balance that compares against standard masses gives the same reading everywhere.)

Change the location from Earth to the Moon to Jupiter (via a planet selector, or by changing the value of g). Watch what each instrument does: the balance stays at 2 kg everywhere, while the spring scale changes — about 20 N on Earth, about 3 N on the Moon, about 50 N on Jupiter.

Write down, for each location, which reading changed and which stayed the same, and state in words why: the amount of matter (mass, kg) never changed, but the gravitational pull on it (weight, N) did.
Answer a prompt such as 'Would an astronaut float away here?' and connect your answer back to W = m×g — smaller g means smaller weight, but the same mass.
Build a short ratio/double-number-line for weight across the planets to show weight is proportional to g while mass is held fixed.
activities.insight: The kilogram reading describes the object itself (its matter); the newton reading describes the gravitational pull on it. Mass is constant with location; weight changes because g changes. W = m×g is a proportional relationship, not a magic triangle.

activities.title: Labelled instruments: which quantity, which unit
steps: Examine a two-pan balance (used with standard masses) and a spring scale/newton meter side by side; for each, reveal (e.g. tap-to-reveal) the quantity it measures and its unit — two-pan balance → mass in kg; spring scale/newton meter → weight (force) in N.
State in your own words why both show numbers but measure different things.
Sort everyday examples by unit: which quantities belong in kg (amount of matter) and which in N (force).
activities.insight: A balance and a spring scale do NOT measure the same thing: one measures the amount of matter (kg), the other the gravitational force (N). Units are not interchangeable.

activities.title: Astronaut interview: weight, mass and 'no gravity in space'
steps: Take part in a spoken or written exchange in the role of (or interviewing) an astronaut: 'Do you weigh less up here? What about your mass? Is there any gravity at all?'
Explain whether the astronaut's mass changes on the Moon or in deep space (far from any planet or star), and whether their weight changes, giving reasons in terms of g.

Address the 'there is no gravity in space' idea: in deep space, far from any large mass, the gravitational pull is tiny so weight is near zero while mass is unchanged; the Moon has gravity about a sixth of Earth's, so weight there is reduced, not zero.

As an optional clarification of the 'no gravity in space' tail (kept qualitative), discuss why astronauts seen 'floating' on the International Space Station are NOT in a region without gravity: gravity there is still strong, and they float because they are in continual free fall — their mass has not changed.
activities.insight: Location changes weight (the gravitational pull) only by changing g, not mass (the amount of matter). Near-zero weight in deep space is different from the apparent weightlessness of free fall in orbit, where gravity is still strong; in every case mass is unchanged and 'floating' does not mean having no mass.

activities.title: Consolidation retrieval: changes on the Moon, W = m×g, units
steps: Categorise what changes and what stays the same when an object is taken to the Moon: mass (unchanged) vs weight (decreases).
Set a value for g with a slider and compute weight with a fill-in W = m × g for given masses.

Answer multiple-choice items contrasting kg (mass) and N (weight/force), where the misconception options — 'both mass and weight decrease' and 'weight is zero on the Moon' — are marked incorrect with feedback.
Explain, for one item, WHY the answer is correct in terms of g.
activities.insight: Secure retrieval of the mass/weight distinction, units, and the proportional W = m×g relationship, while exposing the 'both decrease' and unit-confusion errors.

checkQuestion: An astronaut takes a 6 kg rock from Earth to the Moon. On the Moon, does the rock's MASS change, does its WEIGHT change, both, or neither — and why?
checkAnswer: Its mass stays the same (6 kg) — mass is the amount of matter, which doesn't depend on location. Its weight DECREASES — weight is the gravitational force on it (W = mg), and the Moon's gravitational field strength g is about a sixth of Earth's, so the rock weighs about a sixth as much. So weight changes, mass doesn't.
